video.title: $400 Client Dinner, $200 Deduction: CRA's 50% Meal Rule (handwritten)

sources: CRA — T2125 Line 8523 Meals and entertainment (allowable part only) (canada.ca, page details 2026-08-31) · current · maximum claim is 50% of the lesser of the amount incurred and an amount reasonable in the circumstances; entertainment includes tickets, gratuities, cover charges, room rentals; the limit does not apply when you bill the client for the meal and entertainment costs and show them on the bill (other exceptions: restaurants/hotels, employee benefits, up to six all-employee events a year, charity fundraisers, construction camps; long-haul truckers 80%)
CRA T4127 (Jan 2026) and CPP 2026, via b4/calc.py · 2026 · tax + CPP for a Manitoba self-employed person with $60,000 net income

Calculation (not a CRA rule): b16/calc.py → data.json. 12 client dinners × $400 = $4,800; 50% = $2,400 deductible; $60,000 → $57,600 net income: tax + CPP saved $853.52 (≈$71.13 per dinner); real cost $4,800 − $853.52 = $3,946.48. Dependencies: province, income, whether the amount is reasonable, records. GST/HST input tax credits on meals have their own 50% rule (not shown). Amounts are an example.

yt.description:
A $400 dinner with a client. CRA lets you deduct $200. Why?

T2125 line 8523: you claim 50% of the lesser of what you spent and a reasonable amount. Tips count as entertainment, same limit.

Example (Manitoba, 2026, self-employed, $60,000):
• 12 client dinners × $400 = $4,800
• × 50% = $2,400 off income
• Tax + CPP saved: about $854 (≈$71 per dinner)
• Real cost: about $3,950

One exception: bill the meal to your client and show it on the invoice, and the 50% limit doesn't apply.

Your last client lunch: who paid, you or the client? Tell me below.

Sources: CRA T2125 line 8523; CRA T4127 2026 rates, CPP 2026. Example only; general information, not tax advice.

_vo: A four hundred dollar dinner with a client. CRA lets you deduct two hundred. Here's why. Line eighty-five twenty-three: you claim fifty percent of the lesser of what you spent, or a reasonable amount. Tips count as entertainment, so they fall under the same limit. Our Manitoba consultant is self-employed and earns sixty thousand. Twelve client dinners a year, four hundred each. That's forty-eight hundred spent. Only twenty-four hundred comes off income. Tax and CPP saved: about eight hundred fifty-four dollars. Roughly seventy-one per dinner. So those dinners still cost about thirty-nine fifty. One exception: bill the meal to your client and show it on the invoice, and the fifty percent limit doesn't apply. Your last client lunch: who paid? You, or the client? Tell me below.
